strengths: The central idea is well-motivated and timely: value function estimation is the key bottleneck for exact inference-time reward alignment, and the observation that stochasticity (rather than deterministic flow maps) is required for consistent exploration is crisp and clearly argued.

The two proposed designs are complementary and practically useful: Posterior Diamond Maps (distilling GLASS Flows into a one-step posterior sampler) and Weighted Diamond Maps (turning off-the-shelf flow maps into consistent value-function estimators via renoising plus importance weights). The Weighted variant in particular is attractive because it needs no retraining of the base model.

The theoretical results are largely sound and non-trivial: the consistency proofs (Propositions 4.1 and 5.1), the derivation of the tilted velocity field (10), and especially Proposition 4.3 showing that the Posterior Diamond Map contains an exact one-step sampler of the DDPM time-reversal kernel are nice contributions with complete derivations in the appendix.

Experiments are unusually broad for this line of work: posterior sampling and inverse problems on CIFAR-10/CelebA/ImageNet, plus high-resolution text-to-image on two architecturally different flow maps (velocity-parameterized FLUX and direct-prediction SANA-Sprint). Evaluating on GenEval/UniGenBench++ that are disentangled from the reward models mitigates reward hacking concerns.

The compute scaling analysis (Figures 8-9) is informative: Diamond Maps show a steeper NFE-quality Pareto frontier than Best-of-N and Flow Map Guidance, with the MC-sample count as a novel scaling axis, and the total NFE accounting is spelled out explicitly.
The limitations section is honest and identifies real issues (high variance when prior support mismatches the reward-tilted distribution; inherited error from imperfect distilled teachers).
weaknesses: There is a significant gap between the theory and the method actually used in the headline experiments. The proven consistent estimator of Proposition 5.1 is not what is deployed for text-to-image generation: the implementation drops the analytical weights, uses reward-only softmax weights, unit-normalizes each gradient term independently (D.2.1), applies the Tweedie approximation (25), trapezoidal quadrature for gamma, and a best-of-rollouts selection rule. This is a reasonable engineering compromise, but it weakens the paper's central 'exact/consistent guidance' claim, since the celebrated consistency guarantees do not apply to the configuration producing the main results (Table 1, Figures 8-9).

Novelty is incremental relative to very recent prior work. The GLASS reparameterization (sufficient statistic, time reparameterization, GLASS velocity field) is taken nearly wholesale from Holderrieth et al. (2025), and the Weighted Diamond Map is closely related to the renoising + importance-correction ideas of Sabour et al. (2025a/b) and LATINO. The contribution is the combination (distillation of stochastic transitions into a flow map, plus correction terms), which is solid but builds heavily on these precedents.

Reproducibility is compromised: the code link is an empty placeholder ('Code for our experiments can be found under .'). Given the many non-obvious implementation details (guidance windows, SNR schedules, loss reweighting, initialization networks), the broken link is a material concern for a paper whose practical pipeline involves many unstated approximations.

Some experimental results undercut the claimed advantages: the Posterior Diamond Map has consistently worse FID than the plain flow map at pretraining (Table 3, e.g., 10.74 vs 6.06 on ImageNet), i.e., there is a real quality tax for the posterior model, and the quantitative gains on GenEval/UniGenBench++ are moderate (0.785 vs 0.737 FMG / 0.748 Best-of-N).

Missing baselines: for value-function-based SMC/search alignment, closely related particle methods such as Twist (Wu et al., 2023a), TDS, and Feynman-Kac correctors (Skreta et al., 2025) are discussed but not compared against empirically, which makes it hard to assess the claimed efficiency advantage for SMC.

The paper claims rigorous 'exactness' language ('our method is not approximate but exact', Section 6) that is overstated: all practical results rely on imperfect distilled teachers, finite Monte Carlo samples (often mc=4), and multiple numerical approximations. The asymptotic/ideal-model distinction should be maintained consistently throughout.

Presentation issues: inconsistent labeling of Propositions as Theorems (Theorem 4.3, Theorem 5.1 vs. Proposition 4.3/5.1), a sentence fragment in the Proposition 4.1 proof sketch ('follows and the reparameterization trick'), typos ('th problem', 'compute-optimla', 'classwhile'), duplicated references (Liu et al., Flow-GRPO listed twice), and a reference with no year (Abdolmaleki et al.). These do not obscure the science but indicate the manuscript needed another editing pass.

The comparison between the two designs is left largely as an 'open theoretical question' (Section 5 discussion) without even controlled empirical head-to-head results under matched budgets on the same task, which limits the paper's ability to give practitioners actionable guidance.
